claim: STX1A and STX2 share 63% total sequence homology.
source: STX1A and STX2 share a 63% total sequence homology and a 69% homology in their SNARE domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a factual comparison between the two proteins.

claim: STX1A and STX2 share 69% homology in their SNARE domain.
source: STX1A and STX2 share a 63% total sequence homology and a 69% homology in their SNARE domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a factual comparison between the two proteins.

claim: Overexpression of STX2 can rescue neuronal survival in the absence of functional STX1 by binding to SNAP-25.
source: As expected from the promiscuity of syntaxins in particular and SNARE proteins in general, overexpression of STX2 can rescue neuronal survival in the absence of functional STX1 by binding to SNAP-25 (Peng et al., 2013), although its cognate SNARE partner in non-neuronal intracellular trafficking is SNAP-23 (Abonyo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2013.

claim: The cognate SNARE partner of STX2 in non-neuronal intracellular trafficking is SNAP-23.
source: As expected from the promiscuity of syntaxins in particular and SNARE proteins in general, overexpression of STX2 can rescue neuronal survival in the absence of functional STX1 by binding to SNAP-25 (Peng et al., 2013), although its cognate SNARE partner in non-neuronal intracellular trafficking is SNAP-23 (Abonyo et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Abonyo et al., 2004.

claim: STX2 rescues neuronal survival at a comparable level to STX1A.
source: We quantified the amount of mouse hippocampal neurons in high-density neuronal cultures at DIV8, DIV15, DIV22, and DIV29 for each group and found that STX2 rescues neuronal survival at a comparable level to STX1A (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and D.

claim: STX2 is strongly expressed in model neurons.
source: Furthermore, immunocytochemistry experiments confirmed that STX2, as well as STX1A, is strongly expressed in our model neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: STX2 neurons showed a dramatic reduction in the EPSC amplitude from 4.3 nA (SEM ±0.53) to 0.7 nA (SEM ±0.16).
source: First, STX2 neurons showed a dramatic reduction in the excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) amplitude from 4.3 nA (SEM ±0.53) to 0.7 nA (SEM ±0.16) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: STX2 neurons exhibit a much slower cumulative charge transfer compared to STX1A neurons.
source: A rapid and synchronous release of vesicles was reflected in a much more rapid cumulative charge transfer in STX1A neurons (Figure 1F, black line) compared to STX2 neurons, where the cumulative charge transfer of the response was much slower (Figure 1F, purple line).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The half-width of the EPSC was increased more than twofold in STX2 neurons.
source: Additionally, the half-width of the EPSC was increased more than twofold in STX2 neurons (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: STX2 does not support synchronous Ca2+-evoked release, but a slow asynchronous response.
source: Overall, our results indicate that STX2 does not support synchronous Ca2+-evoked release, but a slow asynchronous response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on EPSC kinetics.

claim: STX2 neurons exhibit a 75% reduction in the RRP of vesicles compared to STX1A neurons.
source: We also evaluated synaptic vesicle priming by applying a hypertonic sucrose solution (500 mM) for 5 s and measuring the charge of the response (Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996) and found that STX2 neurons exhibit a 75% reduction in the RRP of vesicles compared to STX1A neurons (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and cites the method from Rosenmund and Stevens, 1996.

claim: STX2 does not support synaptic vesicle priming to the same extent as STX1A.
source: This suggests that STX2 does not support synaptic vesicle priming to the same extent as STX1A.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RRP data.

claim: STX2-expressing neurons displayed more than twofold increase in the frequency of spontaneous release (mEPSC) relative to STX1A neurons.
source: STX2-expressing neurons also displayed more than twofold increase in the frequency of spontaneous release (mEPSC) relative to STX1A neurons (Figure 1I)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: STX2-expressing neurons showed a 55% increase in the probability of release (PVR).
source: STX2-expressing neurons also displayed more than twofold increase in the frequency of spontaneous release (mEPSC) relative to STX1A neurons (Figure 1I) and a 55% increase in the probability of release (PVR), calculated by dividing the EPSC charge by the RRP charge (Figure 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: STX2 neurons showed a nearly 15-fold increase in the spontaneous vesicular release rate compared to STX1A neurons.
source: When we normalized the mEPSC frequency to the RRP size, we found a nearly 15-fold increase in the spontaneous vesicular release rate in STX2 compared to STX1A neurons (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The increase in the spontaneous vesicular release rate and the PVR indicates that STX2-containing SNARE complexes render vesicles more fusogenic.
source: The increase in the spontaneous vesicular release rate and the PVR indicates that STX2-containing SNARE complexes render vesicles more fusogenic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on release rates and PVR.

claim: STX2 neurons follow a fusion energetic landscape that differs from STX1A and resembles constitutive versus regulated release.
source: Taken together, this data suggests that STX2 neurons follow a fusion energetic landscape that differs from STX1A and resembles constitutive versus regulated release (reviewed by Sørensen, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to Sørensen, 2009.

claim: The N-terminal halves of STX1A and STX2 share 81% homology.
source: Whereas the N-terminal halves of STX1A and STX2 share an 81% homology, their C-terminal halves only share 60% homology (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The C-terminal halves of STX1A and STX2 share 60% homology.
source: Whereas the N-terminal halves of STX1A and STX2 share an 81% homology, their C-terminal halves only share 60% homology (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Replacement of the full-SNARE domain (STX1A-2(SNARE)) or the C-terminal half (STX1A-2(Cter)) of the SNARE domain of STX1A with the same domain from STX2 resulted in a reduction in the EPSC amplitude.
source: Replacement of the full-SNARE domain (STX1A-2(SNARE)) or the C-terminal half (STX1A-2(Cter)) of the SNARE domain of STX1A with the same domain from STX2 resulted in a reduction in the EPSC amplitude (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no change in the cumulative charge transfer in any of the STX1A chimera groups.
source: However, there was no change in the cumulative charge transfer (Figure 2C) or the kinetic parameters of the EPCS, such as half-width (Figure 2D) or rise and decay time (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), in any of the groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The SNARE domain of STX1A may not be directly involved in the regulation of the kinetics of the release.
source: This suggests that the SNARE domain of STX1A may not be directly involved in the regulation of the kinetics of the release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of changes in kinetic parameters.

claim: Neurons expressing STX1A-2(SNARE) or STX1A-2(Cter) exhibited a nearly threefold increase in the mEPSC frequency.
source: Our analysis also showed that neurons expressing STX1A-2(SNARE) or STX1A-2(Cter) exhibited a nearly threefold increase in the mEPSC frequency (Figure 2E), potentially indicating an unclamping of spontaneous release.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The total charge transfer in response to a hypertonic sucrose application was significantly decreased in STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) groups from 0.5 nC (SEM ±0.06) to 0.18 nC (SEM ±0.02) and 0.2 nC (SEM ±0.02), respectively, compared to STX1A WT.
source: Additionally, the total charge transfer in response to a hypertonic sucrose application was significantly decreased in these two groups from 0.5 nC (SEM ±0.06) to 0.18 nC (SEM ±0.02) and 0.2 nC (SEM ±0.02), respectively, compared to STX1A WT, indicating fewer primed synaptic vesicles and a smaller RRP (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A may be directly involved in the clamping mechanism for the spontaneous release of synaptic vesicles.
source: These results suggest that the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A may be directly involved in the clamping mechanism for the spontaneous release of synaptic vesicles and may also play a role in the modulation of the RRP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on mEPSC frequency and RRP.

claim: The C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A may play a role in the modulation of the RRP.
source: These results suggest that the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A may be directly involved in the clamping mechanism for the spontaneous release of synaptic vesicles and may also play a role in the modulation of the RRP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on RRP size.

claim: STX1A-2(Nter)-expressing neurons showed a significant increase from 6.84 Hz (SEM ±0.62) to 11.8 Hz (SEM ±1.28) in the mEPSC frequency.
source: However, it should be noted that we also observed a significant increase from 6.84 Hz (SEM ±0.62) to 11.8 Hz (SEM ±1.28) in the mEPSC frequency of STX1A-2(Nter)-expressing neurons (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: STX1A-2(SNARE) showed a 39% increase in the PVR.
source: We next examined release efficacy in the STX1A-STX2 SNARE domain chimeras. STX1A-2(SNARE) showed a 39% increase and STX1A-2(Cter) showed a 42% increase in the PVR (Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: STX1A-2(Cter) showed a 42% increase in the PVR.
source: We next examined release efficacy in the STX1A-STX2 SNARE domain chimeras. STX1A-2(SNARE) showed a 39% increase and STX1A-2(Cter) showed a 42% increase in the PVR (Figure 2G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) had a 17- and 8-fold increase, respectively, in the spontaneous vesicular release rate.
source: Finally, STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) had a 17- and 8-fold increase, respectively, in the spontaneous vesicular release rate (Figure 2H)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) showed a 40% decrease in the PPR.
source: Finally, STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) had a 17- and 8-fold increase, respectively, in the spontaneous vesicular release rate (Figure 2H), a 40% decrease in the PPR (Figure 2I)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) showed increased depression in a 10 Hz train stimulation.
source: Finally, STX1A-2(SNARE) and STX1A-2(Cter) had a 17- and 8-fold increase, respectively, in the spontaneous vesicular release rate (Figure 2H), a 40% decrease in the PPR (Figure 2I), and increased depression in a 10 Hz train stimulation (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A is involved in the regulation of the efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release, the formation of the RRP, and the clamping of spontaneous release.
source: Taken together our results suggest that the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A is involved in the regulation of the efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release, the formation of the RRP, and the clamping of spontaneous release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on chimeric constructs.

claim: STX2-1A(SNARE) partially rescued the EPSC amplitude compared to STX2, from 0.35 nA (SEM ±0.044) to 2.6 nA (SEM ±0.28), although not to STX1A WT levels 4.06 nA (SEM ±0.31).
source: When recording from the STX2-STX1A SNARE domain chimera-expressing neurons, we observed that we were able to partially rescue the EPSC amplitude when STX2 contained the entire SNARE domain of STX1A (STX2-1A(SNARE)) compared to STX2, from 0.35 nA (SEM ±0.044) to 2.6 nA (SEM ±0.28), respectively, although not to STX1A WT levels 4.06 nA (SEM ±0.31).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on EPSC amplitude.

claim: STX2-1A(Cter) showed a slight, albeit significant, rescue of the amplitude of the Ca2+-evoked response to 1.13 nA (SEM ±0.28).
source: Additionally, STX2-1A(Cter) showed a slight, albeit significant, rescue of the amplitude of the Ca2+-evoked response to 1.13 nA (SEM ±0.28).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on EPSC amplitude.

claim: STX2-1A(Nter) showed a 50% increase in the Ca2+-evoked release to 0.68nA (SEM ±0.08).
source: STX2-1A(Nter) also showed a 50% increase in the Ca2+-evoked release to 0.68nA (SEM ±0.08) (Figure 3B), suggesting an insufficient rescue of the evoked response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A is not enough to support the fast kinetics of the response.
source: STX2 and STX2-1A(Nter) exhibited the slowest cumulative charge transfer (Figure 3C, blue and light blue lines, respectively) as well as the highest half-width (Figure 3D) and rise and decay time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B). These findings indicate that the N-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A is not enough to support the fast kinetics of the response.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on kinetics shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The introduction of the entire SNARE domain or the C-terminal half rescued the speed and synchronicity of the EPSC to almost STX1A WT levels.
source: However, the introduction of the entire SNARE domain or the C-terminal half rescued the speed and synchronicity of the EPSC to almost STX1A WT levels (Figure 3C, dark and light turquoise lines, respectively, Figure 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: There is a dominant regulatory domain which supports the fast kinetics of the response outside of the SNARE domain in STX1A, such as the JMD or TMD.
source: Notably, the speed of release did not change in any STX1A-chimera (Figure 2C and D), suggesting that there is a dominant regulatory domain which supports the fast kinetics of the response outside of the SNARE domain in STX1A, such as the JMD or TMD (Vardar et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to Vardar et al., 2022.

claim: The C-terminal half of STX1A alone is sufficient to evoke faster responses in STX2.
source: However, the C-terminal half of STX1A alone is sufficient to evoke faster responses in STX2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on STX2 chimeras.

claim: STX2-1A(Cter) showed a significant reduction in the mEPSC frequency to almost STX1A WT levels.
source: In line with these findings, STX2-1A(Cter) showed a significant reduction in the mEPSC frequency to almost STX1A WT levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on mEPSC frequency.

claim: STX2-1A(SNARE) showed a 47% increase in the spontaneous release frequency compared to STX2.
source: STX2-1A(SNARE) unexpectedly showed a 47% increase in the spontaneous release frequency compared to STX2, which was also observed in STX2-1A(Nter) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: STX2-1A(SNARE) and STX2-1A(Cter) could rescue the RRP to around double of what was measured from STX2 and STX2-1A(Nter).
source: Additionally, we found that STX2-1A(SNARE) and STX2-1A(Cter) could rescue the RRP to around double of what we measured from STX2 and STX2-1A(Nter) (Figure 3F), albeit not significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F, though the result is not statistically significant.

claim: The suppression of spontaneous release and the regulation of the RRP rely on the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A.
source: These data indicate that the suppression of spontaneous release and the regulation of the RRP rely on the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A, while the efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release depends on the integrity of the entire SNARE domain (Figure 3G, I, and J).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3G, I, and J.

claim: The efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release depends on the integrity of the entire SNARE domain.
source: These data indicate that the suppression of spontaneous release and the regulation of the RRP rely on the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A, while the efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release depends on the integrity of the entire SNARE domain (Figure 3G, I, and J).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 3G, I, and J.

claim: Munc18-1 binds to the N-terminal regions of STX1A.
source: Munc18-1 binds not only to the N-terminal regions of STX1A (Burkhardt et al., 2008; Khvotchev et al., 2007; Meijer et al., 2018) but also to the SNARE complex (Baker et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2018; Stepien et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burkhardt et al., 2008; Khvotchev et al., 2007; Meijer et al., 2018.

claim: Munc18-1 binds to the SNARE complex.
source: Munc18-1 binds not only to the N-terminal regions of STX1A (Burkhardt et al., 2008; Khvotchev et al., 2007; Meijer et al., 2018) but also to the SNARE complex (Baker et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2018; Stepien et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baker et al., 2015; Jiao et al., 2018; Stepien et al., 2022.

claim: The expression levels of Munc18-1 and STX1A influence each other.
source: The expression levels of Munc18-1 and STX1A influence each other, and their interaction is important for priming and release (Gerber et al., 2008; Vardar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gerber et al., 2008; Vardar et al., 2016.

claim: The interaction between Munc18-1 and STX1A is important for priming and release.
source: The expression levels of Munc18-1 and STX1A influence each other, and their interaction is important for priming and release (Gerber et al., 2008; Vardar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gerber et al., 2008; Vardar et al., 2016.

claim: The introduction of the SNARE domain of STX2 into STX1A (STX1A-2(SNARE)) increased the expression of this construct compared to STX1A WT.
source: We found that the introduction of the SNARE domain of STX2 into STX1A (STX1A-2(SNARE)) increased the expression of this construct compared to STX1A WT while the rest showed similar levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The exchange of the entire SNARE domain or the C-terminus of STX1A with that of STX2 caused an increase in the levels of endogenous Munc18-1 at the synapse.
source: Additionally, the exchange of the entire SNARE domain or the C-terminus of STX1A with that of STX2 caused an increase in the levels of endogenous Munc18-1 at the synapse, which may be relative to the increase in STX1A-construct levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with less Ca2+-evoked release.
source: We observed that higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with less Ca2+-evoked release (Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with a smaller RRP.
source: We observed that higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with less Ca2+-evoked release (Figure 4E), and a smaller RRP (Figure 4F)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with higher release efficacy.
source: We observed that higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with less Ca2+-evoked release (Figure 4E), and a smaller RRP (Figure 4F) but higher release efficacy (Figure 4G)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with higher release rates.
source: We observed that higher levels of Munc18-1 seem to correlate with less Ca2+-evoked release (Figure 4E), and a smaller RRP (Figure 4F) but higher release efficacy (Figure 4G) and release rates (Figure 4H)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: STX2-1A(SNARE) and STX2-1A(Cter) showed a trend toward increase in their expression.
source: However, STX2-1A(SNARE) and STX2-1A(Cter) showed a trend toward increase in their expression (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Munc18-1 levels were decreased when expressing STX2 WT compared to STX1A WT.
source: We then quantified the endogenous levels of Munc18-1 at the synapse in these neurons and found a decrease in Munc18-1 levels when expressing STX2 WT compared to STX1A WT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on Munc18-1 levels.

claim: Munc18-1 levels were rescued when either the entire SNARE domain (STX2-1A(SNARE)) or the C-terminal half (STX2-1A(Cter)) of STX1A were present.
source: Interestingly, Munc18-1 levels were rescued when either the entire SNARE domain (STX2-1A(SNARE)) or the C-terminal half (STX2-1A(Cter)) of STX1A were present (Figure 5E and F) compared to STX1A WT neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Higher levels of Munc18-1, observed in STX1A WT and in the STX2-1A(Cter) neurons, showed a trend in increasing Ca2+-evoked release.
source: Our superposition of phenotypes revealed that higher levels of Munc18-1, observed in STX1A WT and in the STX2-1A(Cter) neurons, showed a trend in increasing Ca2+-evoked release (Figure 5G)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Higher levels of Munc18-1, observed in STX1A WT and in the STX2-1A(Cter) neurons, showed a trend in increasing the RRP.
source: Our superposition of phenotypes revealed that higher levels of Munc18-1, observed in STX1A WT and in the STX2-1A(Cter) neurons, showed a trend in increasing Ca2+-evoked release (Figure 5G) and the RRP (Figure 5H)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Higher release rates correspond to groups which show less amounts of Munc18-1 at the synapse.
source: Additionally, we observed that higher release rates correspond to groups, which show less amounts of Munc18-1 at the synapse (Figure 5J).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5J.

claim: None of the mutations caused a change in the EPSC amplitude.
source: The electrophysiological analysis of our point mutations showed that none of the mutations caused a change in the EPSC amplitude (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The double-point mutant STX1AD231N,R232N showed a decrease in the RRP size from 0.469 nC (SEM ±0.08) to 0.19 nC (SEM ±0.03).
source: However, the double-point mutant STX1AD231N,R232N was the only mutant that showed a decrease in the RRP size from 0.469 nC (SEM ±0.08) to 0.19 nC (SEM ±0.03) (Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The double-point mutant STX1AD231N,R232N showed a twofold increase in the PVR.
source: However, the double-point mutant STX1AD231N,R232N was the only mutant that showed a decrease in the RRP size from 0.469 nC (SEM ±0.08) to 0.19 nC (SEM ±0.03) (Figure 6C), as well as a twofold increase in the PVR (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: All mutants showed an increase in the mEPSC frequency; however, it was not significant for STX1AE238V and STX1AV248K.
source: All mutants showed an increase in the mEPSC frequency; however, it was not significant for STX1AE238V and STX1AV248K (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Any small alteration in the outer surface of the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A could destabilize the clamp for spontaneous release.
source: This suggests that any small alteration in the outer surface of the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1A could destabilize the clamp for spontaneous release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on point mutations.

claim: The whole domain is crucial in the regulation of the synaptic vesicle clamp.
source: Therefore, the whole domain is crucial in the regulation of the synaptic vesicle clamp.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on point mutations.

claim: The C-terminus of the SNARE domain of STX1 is crucial in the regulation of multiple aspects of synaptic transmission, such as the clamping of spontaneous release and the formation and maintenance of the RRP of vesicles.
source: We found that the C-terminus of the SNARE domain of STX1 is crucial in the regulation of multiple aspects of synaptic transmission, such as the clamping of spontaneous release and the formation and maintenance of the RRP of vesicles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The C-terminus of the SNARE domain of STX1 is involved in the regulation of speed and efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release; however, these functions are dependent on the integrity of the full-SNARE domain of STX1 and regions outside of the SNARE domain.
source: Furthermore, it is involved in the regulation of speed and efficacy of Ca2+-evoked release; however, these functions are dependent on the integrity of the full-SNARE domain of STX1 and regions outside of the SNARE domain.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: STX1 is fine-tuned for phasic release with a high signal-to-noise ratio for evoked over spontaneous release.
source: Given these findings, and our previous findings which compared the release parameters of the tonic release isoform STX3 with STX1 (Vardar et al., 2022), we argue that STX1 is fine-tuned for phasic release with a high signal-to-noise ratio for evoked over spontaneous release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to Vardar et al., 2022.

claim: The C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1 plays a major role in the stabilization of the primed state and the clamping of the spontaneous release.
source: In this light, we propose a model where the C-terminal half of the SNARE domain of STX1 plays a major role in the stabilization of the primed state and the clamping of the spontaneous release.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: Disrupting the C-terminus of the STX1A SNARE domain by adding that of the non-cognate STX2 may impact vesicle fusogenicity by destabilizing the primed state and decreasing the fusion energy barrier.
source: Disrupting the C-terminus of the STX1A SNARE domain by adding that of the non-cognate STX2 (Figure 7, red dotted line) may impact vesicle fusogenicity by destabilizing the primed state and decreasing the fusion energy barrier that now becomes easier for vesicles to overcome (Schotten et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and supported by citation to Schotten et al., 2015.

claim: Adding the C-terminus of the SNARE domain of STX1A to STX2 may increase the ability of the SNARE complex to stabilize the primed state by increasing the degree of the fusion energy barrier and thereby establish a clamp for spontaneous release.
source: Additionally, adding the C-terminus of the SNARE domain of STX1A to STX2 may increase the ability of the SNARE complex to stabilize the primed state by increasing the degree of the fusion energy barrier and thereby establish a clamp for spontaneous release (Figure 7, light green dotted line).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data.

claim: The SNARE complex is formed by the interaction of plasma membrane-anchored proteins syntaxin-1 (STX1) and SNAP-25 and vesicle-associated membrane protein synaptobrevin-2 (VAMP/SYB2).
source: The SNARE complex is formed by the interaction of plasma membrane-anchored proteins syntaxin-1 (STX1 refers to syntaxin-1A and syntaxin-1B throughout this study unless stated otherwise) and SNAP-25 and vesicle-associated membrane protein synaptobrevin-2 (VAMP/SYB2).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SNARE complex composition.

claim: The SNARE proteins assemble their 55-amino-acid-long, highly conserved SNARE motifs into a parallel four-helix bundle.
source: The SNARE proteins assemble their 55-amino-acid-long, highly conserved SNARE motifs into a parallel four-helix bundle.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SNARE complex structure.

claim: The resulting SNARE complex zippers up sequentially from N- to C-terminus and physically brings the vesicle and plasma membranes together.
source: The resulting SNARE complex that zippers up sequentially from N- to C-terminus physically brings the vesicle and plasma membranes together and provides the necessary energy to mechanically force membrane merger (Fasshauer et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998; Sørensen et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2010; Zhang, 2017; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The assembly of the SNARE complex creates a highly charged outer surface.
source: The assembly of the SNARE complex creates a highly charged outer surface (Fasshauer et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998; Ruiter et al., 2019) to which accessory proteins such as complexins, synaptotagmins, or Sec1/Munc18(SM) proteins can bind to and thereby modulate the efficacy and timing of neurotransmitter release (Rizo, 2022; Rizo and Rosenmund, 2008; Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: STX1-null neurons typically do not survive in culture longer than 8 days in vitro (DIV) and exhibit a complete loss of neurotransmitter release.
source: STX1-null neurons typically do not survive in culture longer than 8 days in vitro (DIV) and exhibit a complete loss of neurotransmitter release (Vardar et al., 2016; Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vardar et al., 2016 and data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: STX2 has been found in brain tissue and is present in the synaptosome fraction.
source: For example, the isoform STX2 has been found in brain tissue and is present in the synaptosome fraction (Chen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 1999.

claim: The N-terminal extreme of STX1 contains the short regulatory N-peptide and the autonomously folded three-helical Habc-domain that are essential for the formation of fusogenic SNARE complexes and the readily releasable pool (RRP) of vesicles.
source: On the N-terminal extreme of STX1, the short regulatory N-peptide and the autonomously folded three-helical Habc-domain are essential for the formation of fusogenic SNARE complexes and the readily releasable pool (RRP) of vesicles (Dulubova et al., 2007; Fernandez et al., 1998; Gerber et al., 2008; Khvotchev et al., 2007; Ma et al., 2011; Vardar et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: STX1 contains the juxtamembrane domain (JMD) and the transmembrane domain (TMD) that are actively involved in membrane fusion.
source: On the C-terminal extreme, STX1 contains the juxtamembrane domain (JMD) and the transmembrane domain (TMD) that are actively involved in membrane fusion (Dhara et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2012; McNew et al., 1999; Sutton et al., 1998; Vardar et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The SNARE motif can be functionally compartmentalized into two subdomains: the N-terminus, necessary for priming and nucleation of the SNARE complex, and the C-terminus, essential for fusion.
source: SNAP-25 and SYB2 mutation studies that destabilize the inner hydrophobic pocket of the SNARE domain have determined that the SNARE motif of these proteins can be functionally compartmentalized into two subdomains: the N-terminus, necessary for priming and nucleation of the SNARE complex, and the C-terminus, essential for fusion (Gao et al., 2012; Sørensen et al., 2006; Walter et al., 2010; Weber et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Single-molecule optical tweezer studies determined the sequential assembly of the SNARE complex through diverse stages assisted by the N-terminal and C-terminal subdomains.
source: This was further confirmed by single-molecule optical tweezer studies, which determined the sequential assembly of the SNARE complex through diverse stages assisted by these two subdomains (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2012.

claim: Munc18-1 and complexin chaperone the stability of the N-terminus and facilitate or clamp the assembly of the C-terminus in the partially zippered SNARE domain.
source: Additionally, it has been determined that accessory proteins, such as Munc18-1 and complexin, chaperone the stability of the N-terminus and facilitate or clamp the assembly of the C-terminus in the partially zippered SNARE domain, which without their regulation is fast and spontaneous (Gao et al., 2012; Hao et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The SNARE motif of STX1 may carry structural features that regulate spontaneous release.
source: Although studies using STX1/STX3 chimeric constructs revealed that the SNARE motif of STX1 may carry structural features that regulate spontaneous release (Vardar et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vardar et al., 2022.

claim: STX2 is implicated in the secretion of various peripheral secretory cells.
source: For that purpose, we used a comprehensive structure–function approach and compared the efficacy of STX1 to the closely related isoform STX2 (Sherry et al., 2006), which is implicated in the secretion of various peripheral secretory cells (Abonyo et al., 2004; Dolai et al., 2018; Hutt et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: When expressed in STX1-null hippocampal mouse neurons, STX2 synapses showed impaired vesicle priming, unclamping of spontaneous release, as well as inefficient and slowed Ca2+-evoked fusion.
source: When expressed in STX1-null hippocampal mouse neurons (Vardar et al., 2016), STX2 synapses showed impaired vesicle priming, unclamping of spontaneous release, as well as inefficient and slowed Ca2+-evoked fusion, consistent with an impaired SNARE complex function (Hao et al., 2023; Jiao et al., 2018; Lai et al., 2017; Stepien et al., 2022; Voleti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The role of the SNARE complex goes beyond zippering and interacting with regulators of release and has evolved to participate in the fine-tuning of the fusion energy barrier and the precision of synaptic vesicle release alongside its accessory proteins.
source: Overall, we discovered that the role of the SNARE complex goes beyond zippering and interacting with regulators of release and has evolved to participate in the fine-tuning of the fusion energy barrier and the precision of synaptic vesicle release alongside its accessory proteins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data.
